title: Why You Need to Check Out October’s Only Winners - Net Growth Media
text:
Why You Need to Check Out October’s Only Winners Why You Need to Check Out October’s Only Winners 0 Share
October is finally and gratefully over. It has been a rough one. But that’s not exactly the case everywhere.
You see, analysts, commentators, speculators and pundits focus on how active markets move. When things are good and everything is going up, certain industries take advantage. When the opposite happens, and stocks generally tank, those same industries collapse the hardest. So, they remain the most newsworthy.
But hot stocks like Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) don’t truly make up the whole market. Sure, they remain two of the largest companies in the world… but they aren’t the world.
With the bear that was October now in the rear-view mirror, the mid-term elections days away and the last two months of 2018 now upon us, let’s look at how different sectors perform at different times.
Before we get to that, however, take moment to think of which industries you feel have done the best and worst over the last month and then the last year.
Got your guesses? Good.
It might not come as a surprise, in such a down month as October has been, technology companies have gotten crushed. For the month, they’ve fallen more than 10%. That’s a harsh 30-day period for any sector. But it was by no means the worst.
Here’s the sector breakdown of the S&P 500 for the month of October:
October Sector Performance of the S&P 500
Source: sectorspdr.com
As you can see, it was rough. But four sectors performed even worse than tech stocks to kick off the fourth quarter: consumer discretionary, energy, industrials and materials.
I’m sure you can guess why these kinds of sectors have taken a tumble. With words and phrases like “correction” and “bear market” on the tongues of every market commentator and financial journalist, companies in charge of making the economy go get hurt. If the economic outlook was a bit better, sectors like materials and industrials would certainly do better.
The other two sectors, consumer discretionary and energy are directly tied to consumer confidence… at least in how they trade. So, it makes sense that when confidence in the economy falls, as it has in October, that these sectors would suffer.
But take a look at the rest of that table. What strikes you the most?
For us, it has to be the only two positive performers: utilities and consumer staples.
Why have these two sectors gone up when everything else has collapsed? Well, it’s in their names. Even if the economy were to hit an iceberg (a subject for another time), everyone will still have to pay their electric bills and buy food. These types of industries chug along no matter what the rest of the market is up to.
With that in mind, let’s take a look back at the last 12 months, rather than just one:
Sector Performance of the S&P 500 (Last 12 Mos.)
Source: sectorspdr.com
As you can see, most of those industries we highlighted first – the ones falling the fastest in October – told a different story when the market was going up. Discretionary and technology stocks were two of the three best performers since November of last year. Industrials and Materials were not, however. This was mostly due to the onset of the tariff wars at the beginning of the year.
Meanwhile, staples moved along nicely – yet quietly – at 5.5%. Utilities slumped a tad, but certainly not enough to break your portfolio. The other thing not taken into account here is that utilities often offer high dividends to make up for its slow price movement. This is something we’ve talked about before . Dividends can’t be overlooked, especial if stocks continue their downward move.
So, what can we take away from this? To us, there are two distinct lessons here:
1. When allocating your portfolio during a sideways or bear market, beware of industries that move proportionate with consumer sentiment.
Tech stocks can be quick-hitting, profit opportunities… but only when the time is right. The same is true with discretionary stocks like Amazon, Nike (NYSE:NKE) and McDonald’s (NYSE:MCD). If markets rebound from here back into their positive territory, these companies will likely bounce faster. If not, however, they could drain down the rest of your portfolio.
2. Boring is better, when nothing looks good.
Just as discretionary spending and high-flying tech stocks get all the negative news stories in bad times, sectors like consumer staples and utilities always just chug along without a headline. If the market remains weak, these kinds of companies are exactly where you want to build up your portfolio allocations.
Speaking of which, the end of the year is approaching. We’re already a month into the last quarter of the 2018. So, it is time to start thinking about how you want to build up your portfolio going into the new year.
